newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish doctors prescribe expensive drugs in protest.
newsitem.headline: Polish doctors prescribe expensive drugs in protest.

text.p: Polish doctors deliberately prescribed expensive drugs to patients and referred simple medical cases to further examination on Tuesday in a protest action to win more pay and funding.

The action, aimed at straining public health sector resources, had won huge support in several provinces, Jacek Wutzow, deputy head of the OZZL union which groups about a third of Poland's 90,000 doctors, said.
In their action, to win a new pay deal and more budget spending, doctors wrote prescriptions for costly imported pharmaceuticals rather than cheap local equivalents.
Some patients with minor complaints were sent for elaborate, expensive examinations, medical sources said.

Wutzow, speaking as doctors in other areas continued to treat only urgent cases, told PAP news agency that if talks with the government on January 15 failed to bring progress, the protest could be stepped up further.
Wutzow said that the union had urged doctors backing the new tactics to disregard spending guidelines set by officials.
"They should carry out full diagnostic procedures and inform patients of their rights as taxpayers," he said.
The tactic exasperated Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz who said that spending money unnecessarily would just harm the interests of patients and the health service.

"Luckily, this noisy protest involves merely a marginal part of the medical community," he told reporters, reflecting differences between officials and union chiefs over the extent of support for the protest.
The doctors have called for budget spending on the health service to rise to six percent of gross domestic product this year, while the government has allocated 4.5 percent.
They seek a collective wage deal for doctors, which would increase their monthly salaries to about 3,000 zlotys (more than $1,000) -- three times the average industrial wage.
The health ministry argues that it does not have the resources to meet the doctors' pay demands but has boosted 1997 budget spending on health by a real 10 percent over 1996.
